cue: The view is wide and blurry, and it runs slowly, then jumps ahead.
rows: Most insects see less than a sixtieth as much detail as people do.
Flies and dragonflies can see a light flicker more than 100 times a second, and one beetle up to 400. People stop at about 60. This view runs slowly and then jumps ahead to suggest the difference.
Bees and some other insects can see ultraviolet light, which people can’t. Phone cameras capture very little of it, so the violet tint in this view stands in for it.

cpd.note: a butterfly and an ant resolve about half a cycle per degree; one figure stands for every insect, though locusts and dragonflies are sharper and fruit flies coarser

rows: Ants are credited with a visual field of about 300 degrees, and a desert locust's two eyes together cover 360. A fruit fly has a blind patch behind about 50 degrees wide. You very likely see nearly all the way around you.
A Heliconius butterfly resolves about 0.49 cycles per degree and a weaver ant about 0.52, where a human reads about 30. You very likely see the world in a mosaic far coarser than a human's.
A locust at its best resolves about 3 cycles per degree. Dragonflies reach about 2, the finest known among insects, and a fruit fly manages about 0.09.

A copper butterfly has four pigments, peaking near 360, 437, 500 and 568 nanometers. A skipper has two, near 440 and 540, and a cockroach has only an ultraviolet one and a green one. You very likely have an ultraviolet receptor, a blue one and a green one.
A monarch butterfly, a Heliconius butterfly and a fire ant each have a cell most sensitive near 610 to 620 nanometers. A red admiral butterfly has none. You may or may not have this red cell.

A skipper butterfly's eye follows flicker up to about 180 to 200 times a second, a housefly's about 230, and dragonflies go past 300. A locust follows only 30 to 40. You very likely see flicker that a human, who stops at about 60, cannot.
A cockroach's compound eyes still steer its walking by moving stripes at 0.005 lux, about the light of a moonless night.

Nobody has measured how much ultraviolet reaches you from bluish and bright surfaces, and no record describes a pupil in your eyes. One set of numbers stands for every insect, though acuity differs by more than ten times from a fruit fly to a locust.

On this trial the colours come from the measured receptor peaks (360, 420, 520 nm). The camera's colours and the display are the app's.

Many insects see the direction in which sky light is polarized, strongest in a band 90 degrees from the sun, and steer by it. With &draw=polar and the motion sensors on, fine strokes show that band from the time, the date and the phone's heading. The latitude is taken as 35 degrees north, and the drawing is the app's.

polar.note: how strongly the polarized band of sky is drawn

rows.title: Sharpness
rows.text: A human reads about 30 cycles a degree on an eye chart, and every insect in this group that has been measured sees far less fine detail than that. If you are a large white butterfly, you read about a quarter of a cycle a degree, if you are a drone fly about half a cycle, and if you are a common green darner dragonfly about 2. For most other species, including the monarch, nobody has measured how sharply you see.
rows.note: Left out interommatidial angles because the acuity figures already make the comparison.

rows.title: Speed
rows.text: A human stops seeing flicker at about 60 flashes a second, and the eyes of the butterfly Danaus chrysippus, a relative of the monarch, still follow it at 165 to 210 flashes a second. Nobody has measured how fast your eyes follow a flicker unless you are in that genus or one of the few other species tested, and that figure stays with the species it was measured in.
rows.note: Left out other species' flicker figures because they cannot travel to this view's other species; no record gives a speed for most of the 1,200 species.

rows.title: Ultraviolet
rows.text: Monarchs, cabbage whites, small tortoiseshells and LD moths each have a color-sensing cell that senses ultraviolet best, and so do the drone fly, the seven-spotted ladybird, a dragonfly, a damselfly and the brown marmorated stink bug. You very likely have one as well. Ultraviolet is light that humans cannot see at all.
rows.note: No wavelength numbers used, since they have no comparison job here and do not carry between species.
